catalog_quote: Mamaindê stress is first of all conditioned by morphology. When the Mamaindê word is looked at as an unanalyzable sequence, stress is impossible to predict. ... Primary stress occurs on the root morpheme alone, while secondary stress can occur both in the root and in the affix classes closest to the root. The affixes that occur in strata/morpheme classes furthest from the root never get stressed, even if their syllable structure would make them candidates for stress. ... This time the pattern is clear. Mamaindê presents a quantity sensitive stress system, in which stress is assigned to every heavy syllable in the root. Primary stress is on the rightmost of the heavy syllables. In cases where there are no heavy syllables within the root, and quantity cannot play its stress-attracting role, primary stress is still right-headed, being located on the right-most light syllable. ... sweep_summary: Mamaindé (mama1278) is in the catalog as weight-sensitive, deciding source Eberhard 2009 (LOT 236, held held by the project and re-read this search of works with stress in the title at pp.140-145; quote verbatim). The three works with stress in the title are the author's 1993 UTA MA thesis, its 1995 SIL/UTA PL 122 book version, and Stonham's 1998 review of it in Word 49(1):134-141. None could be read: the 1993 thesis has no open copy (UTA repository could not be reached by automated download); the 1995 book is search-only on HathiTrust (2 copies) and SIL Global's site is could not be reached by automated download; Stonham 1998 sits inside the paywalled T&F 'Reviews' bundle DOI 10.1080/00437956.1998.11673880. Two further reviews of the 1995 book were found via Crossref: Kenstowicz 1996 (Phonology 13(3):450-455, DOI 10.1017/s0952675700002748) and Price 1996 (IJAL 62(3):314-316, DOI 10.1086/466300). The publisher's first-page preview of Kenstowicz was downloaded and scanned (p.450): it reports the 1995 analysis as closed-syllable weight attracting stress, some closed affix syllables systematically unstressed, and primary stress always on a stem syllable, which confirms the catalog's classification. Eberhard 2009 states (p.140, fn.138) that its basic conclusions equal the 1995 monograph with 'a few crucial differences', so the 2009 grammar remains the best statement and nothing found supersedes it. All items are low/none acquisition priority; everything downloaded is under with. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Books API, scholar.

new_statements.reading: Word stress is computed over the root (stem), not the whole word: every heavy syllable of the root is stressed, primary stress falls on the rightmost heavy syllable of the root, and if the root has no heavy syllable primary stress falls on the root-final (rightmost light) syllable; affixes get at most secondary stress (inner classes, heavy syllables only) and outer affixes never any. weight-sensitive, right-headed, morphologically bounded. This is the same text the catalog already quotes; this search of works with stress in the title produced nothing that outranks it, and Kenstowicz's 1996 review (p.450, read) independently reports the same weight/stem-based pattern for the 1995 analysis that the 2009 grammar explicitly updates.

new_statements.quote: the basic notion is that each heavy syllable has two moras, and foot stress is then assigned to each heavy syllable. Word-level stress is right-headed, or assigned to the rightmost heavy syllable. However, word-level stress can only occur within the domain of the stem. If there are no heavy syllables within the stem, which often is the case, then stress is assigned to the rightmost open syllable of the stem. Secondary foot-level stress is allowed on heavy syllables outside the stem except for the final morphological category of verb suffixes (the person, tense, and mood markers) which cannot carry any stress at all regardless of their weight.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's Eberhard 2009 statement (stem-bounded, rightmost heavy syllable of the stem, else rightmost light syllable of the stem; secondary stress on heavy affix syllables, none on outermost affixes). It adds detail: the phonetic correlates (amplitude, lengthening, vowel quality), the explicit statement that lexical H/L tone is independent of stress, the identification of the unstressable outer class as the person/tense/mood verb suffixes and articles, and the acoustic evidence (250 utterances x 3 speakers, 2001 recordings). Also anchors the same analysis in Eberhard 1995:53, 69.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mamaindê is quantity-sensitive: every heavy (bimoraic, closed) syllable gets foot stress; word-level (primary) stress is right-headed and falls on the rightmost heavy syllable, but only inside the stem; if the stem has no heavy syllable, primary stress goes to the rightmost open (light) syllable of the stem, realized by vowel lengthening. Stress is cued by amplitude, vowel lengthening and vowel quality (p. 6); the language also has lexical H/L tone, and 'pitch is independent of stress' (p. 10) — any of the four tone patterns can sit on the stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary foot-level stress on heavy syllables outside the stem (affixes), except the outermost verb suffixes (person, tense, mood markers), which 'cannot carry any stress at all regardless of their weight' (p. 4); footnote 2 (p. 4) adds that the extra amplitude is also absent on heavy syllables of morphemes at the rightmost periphery of the word such as articles and person/tense/mood markers.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphology bounds the domain: primary stress is confined to the stem; peripheral morpheme classes (person/tense/mood markers, articles) never bear stress. Footnote 3 (p. 6) revises Eberhard 1995: the lengthening of the rightmost open vowel in stems without heavy syllables is now part of the stress rule itself, not a separate post-lexical process. Footnote 6 (p. 6): the related Northern Nambikwara lects Latundê and Lakondê are analyzed by Telles (2002:114) as pitch accent systems with pitch as the only correlate of stress — different from Mamaindê.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2004 paper describes Mamaindê proper (data recorded April 2001 in the village of Capitão Pedro, Mato Grosso, three male speakers). Footnote 6 (p. 6) distinguishes the related Northern Nambikwara lects Latundê and Lakondê, which Telles (2002:114) analyzes as pitch accent systems with pitch as the sole correlate of stress — not applicable to Mamaindê.

sources.quote: Things become a little clearer when weight is factored in: closed syllables are heavy and attract stress while open light syllables are skipped (see below); however, some closed syllables remain systematically unstressed: e.g. the third syllable in wanun-ax-wa 'I am good' and the second in wa-nunta-wa 'you obviously will come'. ... The various Mamaindé stress patterns begin to make sense once the morphology is taken into account. First (putting aside a single exception; see below), one of the syllables of the stem always bears a primary stress: e.g. walekhan-txu 'chief (INDEF)', hala-txu 'land (INDEF)', wet-txu 'child (INDEF)'.
sources.note: Independent metrical phonologist's reading of the same system (cited by Eberhard 2009 fn.138 as 'a helpful review'); useful third-party check on the weight-sensitive unbounded/right-headed analysis and on whether foot-level marks count as secondary stress.
